title: What tells each part what to do
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how an opcode becomes a set of hardware settings, read a control table, and say why decoding is a lookup rather than a computation.

blocks.text: The datapath is wires and units. Nothing in it knows whether the current instruction is an add or a load — that comes from a separate set of signals derived from the opcode, and setting them correctly is what decoding actually is.
The signals a simple design needs

rows: Write back the loaded value or the ALU result?

blocks.title: Decoding is a lookup, not a calculation
blocks.text: That table is the decoder. Given an opcode, the hardware produces the row — and because the opcode sits in fixed bits at the bottom of every instruction, the lookup can begin the moment the instruction arrives. This is why the encoding lesson's point about the opcode's position matters: a decoder that must compute something to find the opcode would put that computation on the critical path of every instruction.
Reading the table as a description of behaviour

items: add and addi differ in exactly one signal: where the second operand comes from
lw is the only row with MemRead and MemToReg set, which is why it is the slowest
sw is the only row with MemWrite set and RegWrite clear
beq sets no data signals at all — it only affects the program counter
Every dash marks a signal whose value cannot affect the result

blocks.text: Read down the columns instead and a different fact appears: each column is one control input on one piece of hardware, and the number of rows that set it tells you how often that hardware is used. MemRead is set in one row out of five, which is a first hint at why the memory stage is worth optimising more than the others.
Where funct3 and funct7 come in

The opcode selects the row; funct3 and funct7 select what the arithmetic unit does within it. add and sub share every control signal in the table — the only difference is one input to the unit itself, which is exactly what the encoding lesson measured as a single bit of difference between the two instructions.

blocks.title: The encoding and the control table are the same design decision
blocks.text: Instructions that behave alike were given adjacent encodings, and instructions that differ in one respect were given encodings that differ in one field. That is not a coincidence to notice afterwards — the encoding was chosen so that the decoder could be small. When you found add and sub differing by exactly one bit, you were looking at the control table from the other side.
Why this scales badly with complexity

With five instruction kinds and six signals, the table fits in a paragraph. An architecture with hundreds of instructions and dozens of addressing modes needs a far larger one, and the logic to produce it is deeper — which puts more delay before anything can start. This is the concrete form of the argument from the RISC versus CISC lesson, and it is why complex designs decode into simpler internal operations rather than controlling the datapath directly.

blocks.expected: A control table you derived rather than read, and a hypothetical memory-arithmetic instruction whose cost you can now state in signals and units. That last exercise is the load-store argument made concrete: the instruction is not impossible, it is expensive in a way you can now count.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can the decoder begin working the instant an instruction arrives?

choices.C: The opcode is in fixed low bits

checkpoint.explanation: The lookup needs no computation to find it. That is the practical payoff of the encoding lesson's field-position rule. A decoder that had to compute where the opcode was would add that delay to every instruction.

checkpoint.prompt: In the control table, sw has a dash for MemToReg. What does that mean?
checkpoint.explanation: A store writes no register — so its value cannot affect the result. MemToReg only selects what gets written back, and a store writes nothing back. Marking it as unobservable lets the hardware simplify that path.

checkpoint.prompt: What distinguishes add from sub, given that they share every control signal in the table?

choices.C: funct7 — one input to the arithmetic unit

checkpoint.explanation: Is the single bit of encoding difference measured earlier. The opcode selects the row; funct3 and funct7 select the operation within it. The one-bit encoding difference and the one-input control difference are the same fact seen from two sides.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a complex instruction set make direct control of the datapath impractical?

choices.B: Control signals are limited to eight
choices.D: Many instructions and addressing modes mean a much larger table and deeper logic, adding delay before anything can start

checkpoint.explanation: It is why complex designs decode into simpler internal operations and control the datapath with those instead, which is the RISC-versus-CISC argument in its concrete hardware form.
